title: skroutz-cli: built for personal AI assistants
description: A terminal client for skroutz.gr that logs into my real account and calls the same MCP server Skroutz shipped for ChatGPT and Claude. Same wire, thinner handle: one binary, 27 tools, no schemas parked in your context window.
body:
It started as scraping. [curl_cffi](https://github.com/lexiforest/curl_cffi) with a Chrome TLS fingerprint got past Cloudflare, session cookies got me a cart, and an order was placed and cancelled purely to see whether it would work. Both of those paths are gone now. [Skroutz](https://www.skroutz.gr) shipped an MCP server a few days ago, the one behind its ChatGPT and Claude connectors, and that is a much better door.

So [skroutz-cli](https://github.com/glogiotatidis/skroutz-cli) logs in with OAuth (dynamic client registration, PKCE, one scope) and calls the same endpoint the connector calls. Search, prices, cart, orders, addresses, returns: 27 tools in total.

The interesting part is the shape. A connector is a capability your agent carries in every conversation, 27 schemas in the context window before it knows whether it needs a price that day. A CLI is a capability it picks up when it does and puts down again: `skroutz search "rtx 5070" --json | jq '.results[0].price'`. Every harness that can run a shell can use it, which is Hermes, openclaw, Claude Code, and whatever replaces them next month. [Anthropic's own numbers](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/code-execution-with-mcp) point the same way: agents writing code against those same MCP servers went from 150,000 tokens to 2,000.

**"MCP is the wire. A CLI is the handle you actually turn."**

It is not the opposite of MCP, just the thinner face on it. Underneath, every command is a JSON-RPC call to Skroutz's server with a bearer token.

Finding the wire was the fun part. The endpoint is in no public directory I could query and some ninety guesses returned 404, so I exported a HAR of my own Claude session with the connector page open, and there it was in the browser's own traffic. Then [Hermes](https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/) on DeepSeek flash wrote the whole thing in one night while I slept: 1,400 lines of Python and 33 tests. The hard part was never the HTTP.

title: Greek TV Streamio: Greek on-demand TV in Stremio
description: Greek stations publish their shows on six different webtv sites with no shared catalog. This addon scrapes all of them, resolves every episode to a direct stream, and serves it to Stremio and Nuvio as static JSON.
body:
Six stations, six webtv sites, no shared catalog: Skai hides the episode list in a JSON blob inside the page, ERT has a real API, the rest are somewhere in between. So I wrote one adapter per station and a [Stremio](https://www.stremio.com/) addon on top.

It currently exports **385 shows and 20,019 episodes**. It answers the three protocol calls, catalog, meta and stream, and every episode resolves to a direct MP4 or HLS URL.

There is no server. A static export writes it all as JSON under `catalog/`, `meta/` and `stream/`, and [GitHub Actions](https://docs.github.com/en/actions) publishes that straight to GitHub Pages: 20,414 files, 10.2 MiB. Every four hours it runs one job per station, with `fail-fast` off so a station that breaks does not take the others down, then merges the artifacts. A normal run reuses the previous show list and stream URLs, so only new episodes cost a request.

Requests go through [curl_cffi](https://github.com/lexiforest/curl_cffi) with a Chrome TLS fingerprint, and the helper honours `Retry-After` on a 429. A daily smoke test resolves a stream, follows the redirect and pulls one segment, which is how I find out a station redesigned its site before a viewer does. Nineteen of those 20,019 episodes come back empty. The rest resolve.

Add the [manifest](https://glogiotatidis.github.io/greektv-streamio/manifest.json) to Stremio and the shows are there, by station or all together.

title: A place for the things I build
description: I'm starting a small timeline to post the things I build, as I build them. Short entries, links, snippets. No comments, no analytics.
body:
I've wanted a place to drop the things I build as I build them. Not a full blog post every time, just a short entry with a link and maybe a snippet. So here it is: a small timeline.

It's a plain static site, no framework, no runtime build. Posts are Markdown files with a bit of frontmatter; a Python script compiles them into the JSON the page reads. No build to break. Adding an entry is a new file and one command.

If you want to follow along, there's an RSS feed.
